strengths: Novel problem formulation distinguishing intent discovery from intent elicitation, well-grounded in cognitive science
Creative hierarchical intent simulator with automatic tree construction from artifacts enabling domain generalization
Comprehensive experimental validation including simulated evaluation, real user study with 75 participants, generalization testing, and behavioral analysis

Meaningful empirical improvements: 10-13% intent discovery gain, 84% user satisfaction (vs 72-78% baselines), 27-44% conversation reduction, consistent pattern of better divergence-convergence balance
Solid technical execution with multiple training paradigms (SFT/DPO/GRPO), thoughtful reward design, and proper handling of user expressiveness constraints
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices including all prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details
Honest discussion of limitations including simulator assumptions, safety risks, and low absolute satisfaction scores with appropriate safety evaluation
weaknesses: User simulator fidelity not deeply validated: intent hierarchies extracted via LLM prompting without human verification of whether they capture real preferences; tangential engagement uses random thresholds with no reported variance
Low absolute performance limits practical impact: only 28-40% satisfaction scores across settings; unclear whether this is task-inherent or framework-fixable

Evaluation methodology concerns: using LLM judges (GPT-5.1) for satisfaction/interactivity introduces error; discovery score normalization (Eq. 4) excludes easy/hard cases making absolute progress assessment difficult
Limited generalization evidence: only 10 artifacts per task type; mixed results with underperformance on data visualization; small total sample (50 examples)

Ad-hoc design choices: random threshold sampling for tangential engagement lacks justification; Equation 5 uses fixed p=0.25 without sensitivity analysis; efficiency penalty cap at 1 not well motivated
Potential circular reasoning: training data generated with reward function; evaluation uses same function to judge success
Experimental limitations: 5-turn conversations are short; COLLABLLM baseline from concurrent work; no ablation studies on reward components; prompted baseline inconsistent across models

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly-formulated problem distinguishing intent discovery from elicitation, grounded in cognitive science literature
Comprehensive experimental validation including simulated evaluation across 3 domains, 5 new domains for generalization, real user study (75 participants), and extensive ablations
Consistent improvements across models and domains (~10% relative improvement in discovery, 32% conversation reduction, 83% interactivity improvement)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices covering all prompts, hyperparameters, intent tree construction, and conversation simulation procedures
Novel operationalization of intent discovery through hierarchical intent trees with response-driven progressive refinement
Strong ethical considerations including safety evaluation, honest discussion of assumptions, and proper human participant treatment
Behavioral analysis demonstrating learned divergence/convergence patterns validate that models discover the intended collaborative strategy
weaknesses: Core assumptions are restrictive (monotonic refinement violated 5.3%, single-dimension focus violated 14.7%) and their impact on real tasks not thoroughly analyzed
Heuristic simulator design choices lack theoretical grounding: tangential engagement uses arbitrary random thresholds from [0,1], fixed probability p=0.25 lacks sensitivity analysis
Intent tree construction via LLM achieves only ~85.7% aspect consistency; the ~15% imperfect pairs could introduce systematic biases into training/evaluation, not analyzed
Simplistic reward design treats all intents equally (R_d = |I_{t+1}| - |I_t|) ignoring difficulty/importance; efficiency penalty capping lacks justification
Modest absolute performance: best discovery ~45-48%, intent satisfaction ~33-38%, limiting practical applicability despite consistent relative gains
Limited scope: all three domains are generative/creative; generalization to reasoning, analytical, or non-creative tasks remains unexplored
Reliance on LLM judges (GPT-5.1) for intent satisfaction without inter-annotator agreement reporting; potential biases not addressed
Technical novelty is incremental, building straightforwardly on existing components (hierarchical trees, simulators, SFT/RL); the key novelty is the latent intent concept
User study is limited in scale (75 participants, creative writing only, ~8 turns per interaction) though results do validate simulation findings
Cross-domain generalization test uses only 10 artifacts per task type, which is quite small for strong claims
